instructions: For each fact, read only the quotes and their context. Verdict `support` when the quotes alone state every part of the claim and of each value, with the same scope and qualifiers; `partial` when a part is missing; `not-supported` when the quotes say something else; `unsure` otherwise. A quote with a `heading` is the value line under that heading on the page: read the two together. Do not use what you remember. A clause, scope, condition or exception of the claim that appears only in the surrounding text and not in the quotes is missing: `partial`. A universal claim (always, every, each, all) whose exception stands in the surrounding text is `partial`. When the quotes support the claim but you can see a sentence that would support it better, still vote on the quotes you were given.

facts.claim: In the resource forest isolation model, you join your FSx for Windows File Server file system to an AWS Managed Microsoft AD setup and then establish a one-way forest trust relationship between that AWS Managed Microsoft AD domain and your existing self-managed Active Directory domain.

qualifiers.scope: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server

evidence.title: Using Amazon FSx with AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory
evidence.quote: You then establish a one-way forest trust relationship between an AWS Managed Microsoft AD domain that you create and your existing self-managed Active Directory domain.
evidence.context: ## Using a resource forest isolation model You join your file system to an AWS Managed Microsoft AD setup. You then establish a one-way forest trust relationship between an AWS Managed Microsoft AD domain that you create and your existing self-managed Active Directory domain. For Windows authentication in Amazon FSx, you only need a one-way directional forest trust, where the AWS managed forest trusts the corporate domain forest. Your corporate domain takes the role of the trusted domain, and the Directory Service managed domain takes the role of the trusting domain. Validated authentication requests travel between the domains in only one direction—allowing accounts in your corporate domain to authenticate against resources shared in the managed domain. In this case, Amazon FSx interacts only with the AWS managed domain. In a Kerberos authentication scenario, authentication requests originating from a corporate client get validated by the corporate domain, which then refers it to the AWS Managed Microsoft AD, and eventually the client presents its service ticket to your FSx for Windows File Server file system. For more information about trusts, see the post [ Everything you wanted to know about trusts with AWS Managed Microsoft AD](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/everything-you-wanted-to-know-about-trusts-with-aws-managed-microsoft-ad/) in the AWS Security Blog. ## Test your Active Directory configuration
headings: Using Amazon FSx with AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory

facts.claim: Shadow copies are not enabled on FSx for Windows File Server by default; to protect your data with shadow copies you must enable shadow copies and set up a shadow copy schedule, and shadow copies are not a substitute for backups.

values.display: enabled on FSx for Windows File Server

qualifiers.scope: FSx for Windows File Server shadow copies

evidence.title: Protecting your data with shadow copies
evidence.quote: Shadow copies are *not* enabled on FSx for Windows File Server by default.
evidence.context:
A Microsoft Windows *shadow copy* is a snapshot of a Windows file system at a point in time. With shadow copies enabled, users can quickly recover deleted or changed files that are stored on the network, and compare file versions. Storage administrators can easily schedule shadow copies to be taken periodically using Windows PowerShell commands.

Shadow copies are stored alongside your ﬁle system's data, and consume ﬁle system storage capacity only for the changed portions of ﬁles. All shadow copies stored in your ﬁle system are included in ﬁle system backups.

**Note**  
Shadow copies are *not* enabled on FSx for Windows File Server by default. To protect the data on your file system using shadow copies, you must enable shadow copies and set up a shadow copy schedule on your file system. For more information, see [Configuring shadow copies to use the default storage and schedule](setting-up-fsx-shadow-copies.md).

**Warning**  
Shadow copies are not a substitute for backups. If you enable shadow copies, make sure that you continue performing regular backups.

**Topics**
headings: Protecting your data with shadow copies

facts.claim: User-initiated FSx for Windows File Server backups never expire, are available for as long as you want to keep them, and are retained even after you delete the file system that was backed up.

values.display: backups of Amazon FSx file systems never expire
retained even after you delete the file system

qualifiers.scope: FSx for Windows File Server backups

evidence.title: Protecting your data with backups
evidence.quote: Your user-initiated backups of Amazon FSx file systems never expire, and they are available for as long as you want to keep them. User-initiated backups are retained even after you delete the file system that was backed up.
evidence.context: Lowering the retention period for automatic daily backups will result in the permanent deletion of backups outside of the new retention window. Ensure that you no longer need these older backups before proceeding. ## Working with user-initiated backups With Amazon FSx, you can manually take backups of your file systems at any time. You can do so using the Amazon FSx console, API, or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). Your user-initiated backups of Amazon FSx file systems never expire, and they are available for as long as you want to keep them. User-initiated backups are retained even after you delete the file system that was backed up. You can delete user-initiated backups only by using the Amazon FSx console, API, or CLI. They are never automatically deleted by Amazon FSx. For more information, see [Deleting backups](delete-backups.md). If a backup is initiated while the file system is being modified (such as during an update to throughput capacity, or during file system maintenance), the backup request is queued and will resume when the activity is complete. To learn how to take user-initiated backups of your file systems, see [Creating user-initiated backups](creating-backups.md).

facts.claim: You can access FSx for Windows File Server file shares from on-premises compute instances using AWS Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN, and from a different VPC, account or AWS Region using VPC peering or transit gateways.

values.display: AWS Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN

qualifiers.scope: FSx for Windows File Server network access

evidence.title: What is FSx for Windows File Server?
evidence.quote: You can access your file shares from on-premises compute instances using AWS Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN.
evidence.context: Amazon FSx is accessible from compute instances with the SMB protocol (supporting versions 2.0 to 3.1.1). You can access your shares from all Windows versions starting from Windows Server 2008 and Windows 7, and also from current versions of Linux. You can map your Amazon FSx file shares on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instances, and on WorkSpaces instances, Amazon AppStream 2.0 instances, and VMware Cloud on AWS VMs. You can access your file shares from on-premises compute instances using AWS Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN. In addition to accessing file shares that are in the same VPC, AWS account, and AWS Region as the file system, you can also access your shares from compute instances that are in a different Amazon VPC, account, or AWS Region. You do so using VPC peering or transit gateways. For more information, see [Accessing data from within the AWS Cloud](supported-fsx-clients.md#access-environments). ## Security and data protection
